Content:
12:15 Though I agree that banning ingredients and hoping the problem goes away is stupid, I also don't think that any policy of this regard will ever be implemented at a scale at which it could actually make a difference. It's way too specific, and the food industry has enough money to push back against regulations that would harm their bottom line.

Seed oils are necessary from the supply chain view, but they are the worst source of fat there is. However, banning them entirely and forcing the entire industry to, avocado oil for example, would just lead to the cheapening of its production and it's processing to become aggressive enough to the point that even a good source of healthy fat would become low quality and harmful. It's happening in India right now with coconut oil without government intervention. Cheap coconut oil is hydrogenated, which basically makes it as bad as Crisco shortening is. Ingredients alone matter, but at scale they do matter less.

Markets will do whatever is necessary to keep and make certain ingredients cheap, even if that involves denaturing said ingredient into not being what it was supposed to be.

Content:
I may not be qualified to say this, but I am not at all of the opinion that overeating is the problem.

I do agree that convenience food is the problem, but my own opinion (and it is an unqualified opinion) is that it is the convenience of the food and not the contents or quantity of the food.  In particular, one of the big differences between home cooked meals and convenience foods is how quick convenience foods are to prepare.  In particular, the slow process of preparing food at home allows time to anticipate the food, which allows the body to prime its digestive processes (e.g. produce more saliva) and so allow better digestive processing of the food.

The other problem I have is the level of criticism of modern diets.  We keep on saying how much more unhealthy modern diets are for us than the diets of the past, yet at the same time we have ever increasing life expectancy.  There are of course many reasons for increased life expectancy, and it would be wrong to say increased life expectancy is all down to better diet, but at the same time the increased life expectancy should cause us to hesitate just a little when we do criticise modern diets.

Author: @Bleep5980
Content:
Hey Adam!

I appreciate all of your cooking videos and the insights you share. I think it would be great to see an update on your video about intermittent fasting. I remember watching your previous video from five years ago, in which you were somewhat critical of diets like keto and Paleo. This makes sense because many of them aren’t beneficial for the long term. However, the benefits can be profound for those practicing intermittent fasting (16:8, 18:6, 20:4, OMAD) while on a calorie deficit.

I just finished watching your episode 43 podcast on intermittent fasting and enjoyed listening to your experience from partaking in it. I've been doing extended intermittent fasting for the past two weeks. Coming from a Muslim household where I didn't strictly follow Ramadan most of the time it came around, I can understand why fasting is prevalent in many major religions—it offers significant mental benefits. Alongside a calorie deficit, reducing glucose intake is crucial for losing body fat, especially those who do not exercise actively. Diet plays a vital role in good health, and understanding your body and the cravings you've developed over the years is key to overcoming them.

Your body can thrive without constant food, like three meals a day or excessive calorie intake. In first-world countries, many ultra-processed foods provide little nutritional value, contributing to the high obesity rates and cardiovascular issues we're facing today. Whether nutritious or not, the foods we consume can lead to increased glucose storage in the liver, which raises insulin levels when we continuously eat. By resisting the urge to eat, we can lower our insulin levels since there's no need to transport glucose throughout our bodies if it isn't there and replaced by ketones. 

I’m not a nutrition expert, but this information is readily available for those eager to understand their bodies' behavior around food. The idea that you must have breakfast, especially in America, is one of the biggest misconceptions, heavily influenced by figures like Edward Bernays, a mastermind in public persuasion. The high-carb, low-fat diet promoted by the food pyramid has significantly contributed to the public health crisis we face today.

I genuinely believe that increasing our awareness of what we consume is key. There’s no magical food or group of foods that guarantees weight loss, because, like you mentioned, all food is nutritious, but most ultra-processed ones aren't. It’s all about having the willpower to avoid excessive eating. If we keep eating, we won't lose weight. We’ll maintain high insulin and glucose levels, making burning fat difficult without significant exercise. 

In just two weeks of intermittent fasting, I've already noticed tremendous improvements in my mental clarity. I wake up feeling refreshed and ready to start my day. My sleep has improved, my mood has lifted, and I’ve begun to appreciate the feeling of hunger as a reminder of the clarity that follows when I resist that urge. Hunger is a hormone signaling that we need food, but we can control our reactions.

The benefits of fasting truly outweigh the consequences of our current eating habits and constant snacking. I loved the podcast video you uploaded a few years ago; it encapsulated much of this information. An updated video with critical health information on glucose, insulin, cardiovascular health, and how fasting can handle these factors, combined with calorie deficits for those aiming to lose body fat, would be incredibly valuable. 

All of these elements come together to create a powerful strategy for maintaining willpower and high energy and reducing the tendency to fall back into old habits and overeat, especially with ultra-processed foods.

Cheers!

Author: @cesarbarbero
Content:
Ultra-processed is an absurd word to describe a food. Bread, a staple food for much of humanity since the Chaldeans, is much more processed than potato chips, as the flour undergoes drying, milling, separation, and oxidation. After mixing with additives (salt, sugar, or malt), yeast is added and it is kneaded (a physicochemical process, not just a physical one), fermented, baked, etc. Potato chips are cut and fried (or baked), and salt is added. However, Monteiro considers them to be ultra-processed. It's a simple ideological label from someone who hates the food industry (specially multinational one). Very strange from a resident of Brazil, a country where a high proportion of the population still goes hungry due to the high cost of simple food. And, as they said in the comments, it supports the thesis that natural is good and artificial (or processed!!!) is bad. A thesis that RFK Jr. also subscribes to, for example. Regarding "bad" ingredients (fat, sugar, salt), in Mexico, Chile, and Argentina, commercial products (e.g., yogurt!!!!) that have excessive fat, sugar, or salt must be warned. There are NO health effects. According to Monteiro, you shouldn't do it with the ingredients. In Argentina, we have a dish made by kneading corn starch with beef fat, fried in beef fat, and sprinkled with sugar. It doesn't require any warning, but it's a bomb of carbohydrates, saturated fat, and sugar. Very coherent!!!. But it is a traditional food, therefore good.  We also have a traditional preserve (of Italian origin), which is salami stored in PIG GREASE. Very healthy!!!! Highly processed but not ultraprocessed because it is not made by a multinational (an important point in Monteiros' rules). 
 In general, the nutritional advice of "government experts" is garbage. RFK Jr. would censor studies now, but that's something the NIH, USDA, and the FDA have been doing since at least 1940, for example, with everyone who said the food pyramid was garbage. 
Oh, and "longitudinal" studies are unscientific, because historical science isn't science. A postmenopausal woman who began the study 34 years ago is now 84. Is she the same woman!!!!? And what's the control group? 
Science allows us to discover, but not to advise.
I am speaking as an experimental scientist with 216 publications (h= 43). You can check it on WoS or Scopus.

Education seems to be the key here. I'm a young adult, and I can say at least for my generation, people don't eat well because they don't know how to cook, and they don't know how to cook healthily. And also they don't know anything about nutrition sciences.

This channel is what gave me the confidence to learn how to cook well for myself. Going just one step above heating pizza pockets in the microwave goes a long way.

Instead of a bowl of sugary cereal, why not just boil 12 eggs to eat for breakfast over the next few days? If you want to make it even more palatable, you can smash the hard boiled eggs between two slices of toast with a bit of mayo, black pepper, paprika, and cumin into what I call an egg smash sandwich. A high protein, low sugar meal, that fills you so you don't get hungry so quickly and eat more than you need. I've started making a recipe book for myself called Bachelor Recipes with the idea being recipes that are so easy that even a bachelor can make them while also being cheap, nutritional, scalable, and tasty.

I've developed some allergies that make it so I can't eat most ultra processed foods and have to basically cook all my own food. By virtue of that, I've literally been losing weight and my body has been feeling healthier.

From my personal experience, I'd say the most basic way you can help your body is limit sugar to 30-40g a day, cut out all trans fats (I make an exception for naturally occuring trans fat present in cheese, but aside from that, I don't get meat or anything that has trans fats in it. Limit saturated fats (I try to have as little as possible but I'd say 8g a day is a decent goal to strive for). 

And finally, learn how to cook your own food. It does not need to be an ultra fancy meal that takes several hours and several pots and pans to cook. This will also save you money and personally I find you can make around 4-6 meals worth of food in 90 minutes, and sometimes even more if you're going really simple like a turkey and mayo sandwich.

Author: @SolaAesir
Content:
You really need to work on your research skills. The food and health apparatus is under pretty extreme regulatory capture (a hard left talking point even as recently as 2015). That means that most of the studies that come out are funded, if not done directly, by the food industry. People at all levels of government are beholden to the food industry. Even getting papers published means going through a peer review process that is controlled by the food industry and their money. You can't just do a cursory search of the literature and take the abstracts/conclusions for granted, you have to actually understand the methods and analysis to figure out if the study is giving the result it claims (frequently it's actually a best/worst case boundary), because peer review is never going to do that for you. 

If you aren't able to do that research yourself, you need to at least find the scientists raising issues with the status quo to understand and evaluate the legitimacy of their actual arguments yourself. You inadvertently spread a lot of misinformation/disinformation in this video by giving a strawman of the actual arguments being made about seed oils, processed foods, etc, and additionally by quoting some old nutritional knowledge that has been pretty thoroughly disproven relatively recently as fact.

Author: @SWNJim
Content:
This is why how you define things is important. When you’re reading this, I was thinking biltong or low sugar beef jerky. It’d be the same for any other dried or preserved product. 

Food science has always had problems. It relies too heavily on self reported survey data collection and they do little to account for things skewing their data such as “healthy user bias.” Then they come up with correlative results which get passed off as if they are on the same level as if they are causation, but the most egregious is conflating ABSOLUTE risk vs RELATIVE risk. When they say “eating bacon raises your risk of getting colorectal cancer that doesn’t mean I go from 4.5% (lifetime) to 24.5%, it means that I’m going from 4.5% to 5.4%. For a .9% increase, I’m eating my damn bacon. 

We need better food science in all phases and unfortunately we’re not going to get it with this administration. We also need better definitions that actually separate into distinct categories, probably based on additives.

You complaining about the Trump budget cuts is a lack of understanding of the real issue here.  Budget figures on their own are a terrible way to determine the success of anything.
The best way to determine the success of something is to measure how many positive outcomes there were per dollar spent.  Scientific research and other things need to become more effective and less bloated.  Throwing more and more money at something often only leads to waste, bloat and less outcomes overall.

Budget cuts, in science are not a good or a bad thing. You need the context.  It's how many outcomes per dollar spent that matters.  Having the optimum amount of funding to increase the number of outcomes while still keeping the research affordable in the wider budget.  We need to make scientific research more efficient, not more bloated and wasteful by throwing far too much money at it.

Content:
Yeah, no the terminology & the scale are useless, because there is no actual underlying rule to classify a given food, it's all subjective nonsense by the people who put together the scale.

Detergents ALSO occur naturally in nature... and one of the key traditional ingredients to handmade soaps is lye... an incredibly caustic & toxic substance. 

IMHO, technology is NOT the 'opposite' or negation of nature, technology is the intelligent application of observations to harness nature for the best benefit. Content: Adam! While I do understand a component of this is that the context, convenience, and long-term habits these foods form in diet cause damage beyond themselves, we also have to understand that a big issue is the macro content. These are not nutritious foods, these are not foods with balanced macros; they tend to be INCREDIBLY carb heavy, sometimes fat heavy, using the cheapest possible sources of those macros available. It's incredibly easy to talk about changing what's available in the diet.. but the reason these foods are so incredibly cheap is that they work with the current logistics and staple crops in the US. We produce CARBS, lots of CARBS in the form of corn, grain, and even rice. It starts in the farms, and with what is convenient and accessible.

I'm of the mind that the reason the US *isn't* really addressing dietary issues, is because to do that, they have to open the pandora's box of totally ripping apart the food supply chain at the seams, starting with farmers who surely won't be happy, along with everyone else along that chain. Author: @HumbertoRamosCosta
Content:
I agree that it's hard to define what constitutes "ultra-processed food," but I think that during WWII, the U.S. created a massive factory system to support the war effort. The primary goal was to produce food that was "easy to digest" and "calorie-rich" for soldiers. After the war, facing lower demand, these factories began advertising the benefits of "convenient food." This shift was also aided by the fact that more women began working outside the home.

The key point (to me) is that factories can produce "more calories for the price" than the average person cooking at home, and this—combined with our natural tendency to seek the least effort—has led to the current trend. Additionally, there are developed countries with (what I consider) better food strategies than the U.S., such as France, Italy, Japan, and others.

Author: @benjaminvis
Content:
This was very enjoyable to listen to and very insightful from what I could tell. I'm amazed at the enormous impact such a relatively simple descriptive categorisation of foods has had, but as you point out, there is utility to it. Indeed, it is surprising that when the author did consider ingredients to be a category, it took abother publication to add the ultraprocessed category. One does wonder if there could be sense to refine the categories between processed abd ultraprocessed to become more useful overall. There may also be some conceptual slippage in the terminology, as the category naming indicates that the way foods were approached was not really behavioural nor contextual, but focused on what was done to make and present the food. Nonetheless, there seems to be intuitive utility in the categories on the level of individual behaviour. Cutting down on snacking and treats from ready-made products as well as soft drinks seems like a great way to have some real impact on one's ultraprocessed intake. Yet, without further clarification, it seems unlieky that everything hermetically sealed and packaged to have a long shelf life is ultraprocessed, and where are the lines between basic ingredients off the shelf (half products, if you like) and ready-made sauces (which I'd expect to be ultraprocessed)? The same might apply to seasonings and sandwich fillers, or what to think of (semi)prepared meats and most meat replacements. In other words, even if not specifically on quantifying ingredients, isn't there a way to identifying the kind of processing that constitute worrying types of products that would help make more informed choices when doing the shopping? Is all convenience in the kitchen bad? I'm convinced that depending in what was bought, not all home cooking is good or better than prepackaged foods. It seems entirely feasible to me to cook with a variety of ultraprocessed foods that one the plate come to masquerade as normal processed foods. And are there things we could do in the kitchen that would essentially lead to something very similar to ultraprocessed foods?

You certainly made me think a bit deeper about the subject I only ever took a passing interest in.

Processing is natural, and in many cases essential given how our bodies have evolved - cooking meat, making cheese and butter all count as processed, and this is in no way an issue. Ultra-processing refers to industrial processes being applied to strip base foods down to their components parts and reconstituting them chemically into entirely new foods.

He puts forward a compelling argument for how these new ultra-processed foods are specifically designed to maximise ease of consumption and lead to significantly higher calory intake, including the impact these foods can have (even within a month) of physically rewiring the rewards systems and hormone levels in the brain.

It's really accessible, and has frankly led a gradual but massive shift in how I (and people I've recommended him to) view food. Author: @AndyBHome
Content:
Borderline obese, or borderline overweight? I think that might have been an error. 

BMI stats about health risk hold up well and better than stats about adiposity. BMI is a much better predictor of disease, even for people who are muscular and physically active, than any stats about adiposity. Yes it's absolutely true that people who exercise have better health outcomes on average than people who are sedentary, but people who exercise see exactly the same increase in disease, on average, when their BMIs are in the statistically less healthy groups than their equally exercised counterparts in healthier BMI categories. I think Adam is falling for the wishful thinking that no one has ever considered what BMI stats mean for people who are otherwise healthy. The reality is that it has indeed been studied and the results are pretty clear. Being otherwise healthy does not mean the BMI no longer applies you in terms of statistical risk for disease. Statistically speaking, BMI is one of the most consistent predictors of disease, independently of all other factors. Again, being otherwise healthy is extremely helpful, but it doesn't mean the BMI scale no longer has meaning for your health risks. You may be less likely to get arthritis if you exercise. But being overweight STILL increases the chance that you'll develop arthritis over other people doing exactly the same exercise but at a lower weight. The longer that the BMI is around, the more evidence we get that the BMI is a useful and consistent measure for predicting disease. It's not the only factor of course. Being sedentary is probably worse than having a BMI over 25. Keep in mind that BMI is a predictor of disease that is independent of other predictors. Smoking, high cholesterol, drinking excess alcohol, family history, emotional stress, and not exercising are all big factors that affect health outcomes, but having good or bad scores on any of those accounts makes no difference to the added or reduced risk of BMI. It is not the only tool in predicting disease, but nothing anyone does can reduce its usefulness as a measure of risk for an individual. It's never enough by itself but it's also never irrelevant. 

There does seem to be one aspect of BMI that has been shown to lose it's accuracy for certain people. East Asians seem to have an "overweight" risk starting well below 25. The measures were originally created for Europeans and research has shown that the negative effects of being overweight may start as low as a BMI of 23 for people of East Asian ancestry. Studies looking for the same kind of shift between men and women have proven fruitless so far. Even though women have higher BMIs on average they also live longer on average than men. But again, when the other factors are removed from the equation, your find that women with healthy BMIs live longer, and healthier, than women in less healthy BMI categories. It's a single measure among many that is helpful no matter what else is going on with someone's health. It's not necessarily the most important. It's just always meaningful, no matter what else is going on. 

And we should not forget that the overweight category is associated with clear but very limited increases in risk. It is the obesity categories where health outcomes become significantly impacted. Being in the "overweight" category is far less meaningful than most other disease predictors such as cholesterol, high blood pressure, family history, and exercise. Even waist circumference is a more meaningful measure than having an "overweight" BMI. Being in the "class 1 obesity" of BMI on the other hand is significant and should be considered a sign of risk worth actively addressing. A high BMI is truly the three "obesity" classes, not the "overweight" class, and not high in the "healthy" class. 

People are very sensitive about their weight. BMI is a measure that can help you predict your risk of developing certain diseases. It does not tell you if you're healthy now or not. It does not replace any other test of a person's health. It is one measure among many, but no health condition makes the BMI irrelevant. It's usefulness for predicting disease applies to absolutely everyone, even if the implications are relatively low.

I was once talking with my mother about diets and she insisted she barely ate anything fatty because she talked only about how much oil or butter she used in cooking. When I pointed out all her snacks and snacking habits -- daily palmiers, lots of popcorn, etc. -- she was surprised because she had simply forgotten that she'd eaten those and that those things had fats and carbs, too. Same thing happens with some of my closest friends who also have unhealthy diets (though sometimes in different directions); when they actively think about what they will eat for a given meal, they often make healthy choices...but the problem is that they don't put in this same effort with this snacks, don't monitor or moderate how much they eat when they snack, and sometimes even forget that they snacked at all (or at least what they snacked on). Anecdotally, it's the same process with addiction to actually addictive substances -- it becomes a problem not when people take it, but when they take it so much that it becomes the background noise of their lives and/or they forget they're even taking it in the first place. Milkshakes are obviously not as inherent addictive as heroin, but I do wonder about the neurological impacts or dopamine production of people who thought they "only had a handful of chips" when they ate half the bag at once vs people who thought they "only had a couple of drinks" when they actually got blackout drunk.

Author: @Tinil0
Content:
Man, I really wish more people understood the difference between metrics that work as an aggregate and metrics that work to label individual things/people and how both can be useful for different reasons and even contradictory!  

This comes up a lot especially with the term "healthy", I see so many people labeling individual food items as "healthy" or "unhealthy" and it's so absolutely silly and misleading.  DIETS can be healthy or unhealthy, but individual food items, assuming they aren't literally toxic, aren't by themselves healthy or unhealthy.  They make up a part of your diet and can ALMOST UNIVERSALLY be either good or bad depending on the context of your entire diet as well as you individually and your health issues.  There are obviously a few counter examples, where there are just so many calories that if you finish it one sitting you are over your daily recommended caloric intake, but for the most part ANYTHING can be a part of a healthy diet.  "Giant slice of chocolate cake" isn't "unhealthy", it's only "unhealthy" in the context of eating another 2000 calories across the entire day and additional sugar from other stuff.  Even "Empty calories" aren't inherently bad, they just eat up a lot of your caloric budget without providing any benefit in other categories of things you need.  And even supposedly "healthy" superfoods can be terribly unhealthy in certain contexts, for instance I have Crohn's disease and fiber can easily cause an intestinal blockage so a lot of vegetables are unhealthy to my body despite having lots of nutrients.

It seems like a minor distinction, but the problem is people start getting all sorts of crazy disordered ways of eating by focusing on eating "healthy" food and never eating "unhealthy" food and basically miss the forest for the trees, causing way more harm to themselves than if they had a more nuanced understanding of diet.  For whatever reason, diet is one area where people start becoming ultra irrational, dogmatic, and militant about the strangest things.

Content: NOVA is honestly a copernican revolution in nutritional epidemiology and dietary advice. There are a epistemological consequences to adopting different taxonomic systems. In nutrional epidemiology, classifying food consumption patterns according to NOVA instead of according to major macronutrients finally began to produce clear associations with obesity, morbity and mortality. Skyrocketing non-communicable diseases (which could not be explained by either excess fat intake or excess sugar intake) finally made sense.  When it comes to dietary advice, NOVA is an answer to the "food pyramid" and the notion of portioning food according to their main macronutrient. Education on discerning "processed" from "ultraprocessed" can make a huge difference in food choices that lead to a healthier life.

Author: @ymi_yugy3133
Content:
I think the concept of "ultra-processed" food is highly misleading to the point of being more harmful than useful.
It's very clearly not just used to make population wide studies but as a tool to inform specific dietary decisions and policy. Same thing happens with BMI, e.g. many guidelines for the new weightloss drugs prescribe specific BMI thresholds. 
This does sometimes go pretty wrong. See the whole red meat and raw milk craze or things like tofu sometimes being categorized as ultra-processed.
It's also not like there aren't other good indicators that categorize these foods, like containing some combinations of high sugar, fat or salt.
UPF is also a bad measure in other ways. For one it's not easy to measure and every publication will classify foods differently making comparison very difficult.
So what you get is a measure that's useless for making personal choices because it has to many faults.
It's bad for studying people at a population level because it's not comparable and needlessly biased against certain cuisines. 
It plays right into the interests of some powerful lobby groups like meat and dairy producers.
Optimizing for it leads to many unhelpful adaptations, e.g. a producer might cut out preservatives which might increase food waste without making it more healthy.

Author: @level10peon
Content:
I appreciate you highlighting the nuance of generalizations versus particulars, because this is something that I think many people lose sight of when discussing ultraprocessed foods. Yes, in general, ultraprocessed foods are worse for you than the alternatives. But that doesn't mean in every particular case they are.

For example, it's probably healthier to drink an ultraprocessed whey protein shake than it is to drink a minimally processed, organic fruit juice. The former has protein while the latter has mostly sugar. Another example is it's (at least debatably) healthier to drink unsweetened ultraprocessed oat milk than it is to drink minimally processed whole milk, as the former is lower in calories and saturated fat.

But I've definitely met people who will happily eat and drink very unhealthy foods as long as they're not ultraprocessed, which I don't think is the correct takeaway from that research.
